name: Emeka Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you tell me stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. So you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on an underground cable crew in the city centre. Most people think lineworkers are all up poles, but in the city the power lines are under the pavement, so I spend my days in pits and trenches, jointing cables. Jointing is where you join two cables together so they carry power safely, and it's fiddly, careful work, a bit like surgery in the mud. I start at seven, and one week in four I'm on the night rota for faults.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy a good clean joint, honestly, when you know it'll sit there for forty years. What wears me down is traffic, permits and the night calls, getting out of bed at three because a digger went through a cable outside a supermarket. I've got a little routine with the AI on my phone now and then, it translated the manual for a new German jointing kit last month, but mostly it's just me, my mate Pavel and the cable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, gently. At work there's always someone who's sure the next thing will change everything, and usually it changes the paperwork. I'd say it's useful for small jobs and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I work to sixty-five like I planned, and the money keeps coming in. Hanne and I would keep helping the boys towards house deposits. That's the main thing I'm working for now, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as normal. Use the phone for the odd manual or a letter to the council, keep the night rota until sixty, then come off it as the agreement allows. Keep putting a bit into the index funds every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Relieved, maybe, because I've got a plan and it still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've used AI to translate a manual. Is that the sort of thing you'd expect in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exactly that. Small handy things. It saved me an afternoon with a dictionary. That's nice, but it's not going to dig a trench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your plan to sixty-five look like if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seven more years. Three on nights, four on days. I've got a figure in my head for each son's deposit, and by sixty-five both should be done. Then it's Hanne's turn, she wants to see her sister in Canada for a month.

S0.say: I told you so, gently. AI is useful for small jobs, and usually the big change everyone predicts turns out to be more paperwork.
S0.think: For me it means I work to sixty-five like I planned and the money keeps coming in. Hanne and I would keep helping the boys towards house deposits.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, using AI for the odd manual or letter. Stays on the night rota until sixty and keeps paying into his index funds each month.
S0.feel: Calm and relieved that his plan still holds.
S0.quote: It saved me an afternoon with a dictionary. That's nice, but it's not going to dig a trench.
S0.fieldNote: Emeka works for a clear purpose: helping both sons with house deposits by sixty-five. He uses AI in small, practical ways and sees no threat here. His calm comes from having a plan that this scenario leaves intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real but it's not the end of the world. At work I'd tell the lads to keep an eye on what the planners and the office are doing, because that's where it starts. I'd try to be the sensible one in the canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my job's fine. Nobody's sending a computer down a wet pit to joint an eleven-thousand-volt cable. What bothers me is Tobi, my older son, because his job is exactly the kind of thing that shrinks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the company shows us something that works and then learn it properly, probably the fault-location software. I'd have a long talk with Tobi and suggest he gets a qualification that puts him with clients, not spreadsheets. And I might bring forward his house deposit, so he's not borrowing more just as his job wobbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for Tobi, if I'm honest. My own bit feels solid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned Tobi. What does he do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's a junior accountant at a firm that does company accounts. He's thirty-two and good at it. But half of what he describes to me sounds like exactly what these programs do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you push the AI tools at work, or wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wait, then learn. I'm not the first one in the queue but I'm not the last either. When Pavel starts using something and it actually saves him time, that's when I pick it up.

S1.say: It's real, but it's not the end of the world. Keep an eye on the planners and the office, because that's where it starts.
S1.think: I think my own job's fine, because nobody's sending a computer down a wet pit to joint a high-voltage cable. What bothers me is my older son Tobi, whose job is exactly the kind that shrinks.
S1.do: Waits until the company shows a tool that works, then learns it properly, likely the fault-location software. Advises his son to move towards client-facing work and considers bringing forward his house deposit.
S1.feel: Uneasy, mostly on his son's behalf.
S1.quote: When Pavel starts using something and it actually saves him time, that's when I pick it up.
S1.fieldNote: He separates his own safety from his son's exposure quite clearly. His adoption rule is concrete: he follows his crewmate once it's proven. The idea of moving the deposit forward shows how money and family plans are tied together for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's not panic, let's see what the company actually does. Online I might share something about the government needing a plan. I'm not a placard person, but I'd want someone in charge to say something sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. I'd be sixty in 2028, and if a robot can do jointing, I'm out five years before I planned. Both boys could lose work at the same time, Tobi first. And everything we've saved is partly in shares, which could go anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd sit down with Hanne and the numbers. I'd move part of the index funds into plain savings so it's not all riding on the market. I'd give Tobi his deposit now, not in three years, and I'd ask the company about early retirement terms before the rush starts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's like a fault call at three in the morning where they can't tell you what's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years do to the house deposits?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means doing them now or not at all. Ade's a physio, so his job's hands-on and maybe safer for a while. Tobi gets his now. Ade might have to wait, and I'd hate telling him that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine, but you'd also sell funds and stop the nights. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. We'd be fine for food and the house is ours. It's the plans that wouldn't be fine, the deposits and Hanne's month in Canada. I'd be cutting risk, not cutting meals.

S2.say: Let's not panic and see what the company actually does. I'd want someone in government to stand up and say something sensible about a plan.
S2.think: I'd be worried. I'd be sixty in 2028 and out five years early if a robot can joint cable, both sons could lose work, and part of what we've saved is in shares that could go anywhere.
S2.do: Sits down with his wife in the first month and moves part of the index funds into plain savings. Gives his older son his house deposit straight away and asks the company about early retirement terms before others do.
S2.feel: Anxious, like a fault call where nobody can say what's wrong.
S2.quote: Tobi gets his now. Ade might have to wait, and I'd hate telling him that.
S2.fieldNote: The calm public line covers real private worry. His fear isn't hunger but the collapse of his plans for his sons. He chose between his two sons out loud, which was hard for him to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a bit of time, so use it wisely. I'd tell the younger lads to watch which jobs the machines take first and get ahead of it. Calm, but not asleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'm sixty-three, two years short of my plan. That's not a disaster. I really think I'd get most of what I wanted for the boys done, just squeezed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and save harder, maybe a few hundred more a month, so the deposits are done by sixty-two. Once the company starts testing the machines, I'd learn whatever I need to stay useful to the end. And I'd keep Tobi thinking about his next move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's tight, but it's a plan you can still steer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years is the difference between rushing and planning. With two I'm giving Tobi money in a panic. With five I'm doing it in order, and Ade gets his too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn to work alongside the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if it's proven. If the company puts a machine down the pit and it works, I'd rather be the one checking it than the one sent home. I'd want to see it work a dozen times first, though.

S3.say: We've got a bit of time, so let's use it wisely. Watch which jobs the machines take first and get ahead of it.
S3.think: By 2031 I'm sixty-three, two years short of my plan, which isn't a disaster. I really think I'd get most of what I wanted for the boys done, just squeezed.
S3.do: Keeps working while saving a few hundred more each month so both deposits are done by sixty-two. Learns the new machines once the company tests them, and keeps nudging his son to plan his next move.
S3.feel: Uneasy, with a sense that things are tight but still steerable.
S3.quote: With two I'm giving Tobi money in a panic. With five I'm doing it in order, and Ade gets his too.
S3.fieldNote: He measures the warning time by what it does to his sons' deposits. Three extra years turn panic into order for him. He's willing to work with machines once he has seen them prove themselves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so nobody has an excuse. I'd probably say the government and companies should agree a sensible plan for retraining. Nothing dramatic, just sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, nothing. I'm sixty-eight in 2036, retired three years. The deposits are done, Hanne's been to Canada. I'd just want the boys to have used the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my plan exactly as written: nights until sixty, days until sixty-five, the monthly money into the funds. I'd help Tobi pay for a course in the first year if he wants to switch to something safer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's far enough off that it's the boys' problem more than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would you be in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retired, probably fixing Ade's kitchen. Maybe on a train somewhere with Hanne.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tobi in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him he's got ten years, which is more than most people get for anything. Pick something with people in it, and start now, not in year nine.

S4.say: Ten years is a fair warning, so nobody has an excuse. The government and companies should agree a sensible plan for retraining, nothing dramatic.
S4.think: For me, nothing changes, because I'm sixty-eight in 2036 and retired three years. I'd just want the boys to have used the time well.
S4.do: Follows his plan exactly, working nights until sixty and days until sixty-five while paying into his funds. Offers to help his son pay for a course in the first year if he wants to switch.
S4.feel: Calm, since it feels like his sons' problem more than his.
S4.quote: Pick something with people in it, and start now, not in year nine.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years places the change safely after his retirement, so his attention moves fully to his sons. His advice is practical and specific. A centrist who wants sensible plans rather than drama.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt. It lands on me, Tobi and the savings all at once. What would help is a proper bridge to the pension for people my age, and some steady advice for people like Tobi on what's actually safe to move into.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what I'm working for. People assume it's for me. At my age it's for the boys. If you asked a hundred men my age on the crews, I bet most would say the same.

headlineQuote: It's fiddly, careful work, a bit like surgery in the mud.
portrait: Emeka Jensen is a 58-year-old underground cable jointer on a city crew who works for one clear goal: helping both his sons with house deposits before he retires at sixty-five. He uses AI now and then, for a translated manual or a letter, and picks up new tools once his crewmate Pavel proves they work. He feels his own job is safe in the milder scenarios and worries mostly about his older son Tobi, a junior accountant. AGI by 2028 makes him anxious because it would hit him, Tobi and his invested savings at once, and he'd have to choose which son gets help first. With more warning, his plans become steerable again.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because it would hit his own job, his son Tobi's job and their savings all at once.
whatWouldHelp: A proper financial bridge to the pension for workers his age, and steady advice for people like his son on which kinds of work are safe to move into.
